description: A comparative and system-level study of national AI capacity, relational boundary control, target-side autonomy, and systemic influence within the emerging global AI power order.
abstract: This book examines how artificial intelligence capabilities become consequential forms of power under uneven technological interdependence. It distinguishes AI National Power (ANP), the conversion of resources into nationally usable capacity; AI Boundary Power (ABP), effective relational control over access to consequential AI-related functions; Boundary Autonomy, the capacity of affected actors to establish credible alternatives; and Systemic Influence, persistent, sufficiently broad, and credibly attributable structural change. Drawing on a structured comparison of thirteen principal national AI systems across five functional domains, the study examines capacity conversion, resource dependence, institutional organization, and operational maturity. It assesses semiconductor and computing boundaries alongside model, cloud, platform, data, procurement, market-access, regulatory, talent, capital, and security interfaces, and maps technological domains, international networks, strategic nodes, and overlapping regional configurations, including ASEAN. The evidence supports an emerging global AI order that is uneven, polycentric, and non-exclusive rather than a single national ranking or partition into mutually exclusive blocs. All eight candidate Systemic Influence claims remain Not Adjudicated under the specified evidentiary requirements; this is not evidence that their effects are absent. The empirical classification cutoff is 30 September 2026. The accompanying Research Supplement documents detailed evidence registers and adjudication decisions corresponding to the book's empirical classifications.
